newsitem.title: USA: Federal terrorism team to train U.S. cities.
newsitem.headline: Federal terrorism team to train U.S. cities.

text.p: Federal experts have gathered in Denver to kick off a programme to prepare 120 U.S. cities to respond quickly to terrorist incidents such as chemical and biological attack, the Pentagon said on Wednsday.

The three-year disaster plan, ordered by Congress and headed by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), was using Denver as a pilot because it expressed strong initial interest in the programme, defence officials told reporters.

Denver, with the nation's second largest federal bureaucracy, was currently the site of the trial of Timothy McVeigh, accused of bombing the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in Oklahoma City in 1995, killing 168 people.

The city will also play host to a June 20-22 summit of the Group of Seven (G7) nations, the world's leading industrial democracies. The leaders of Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States will attend.
A team of about a dozen federal officials arrived in Denver on Monday to begin assessing preparedness and training of local fire officials, police and other emergency personnel.

In addition to FEMA, agencies represented on the team are the FBI, Energy Department, Environmental Protection Agency, Public Health Service and Defence Department, the defence officials said at a Pentagon briefing.

The officials, who asked not to be identified, said military experts on chemical and biological warfare would play a key role in advising police and others in areas such as identifying chemical agents and moving and treating attack victims.
But they stressed that FEMA was heading the effort and that troops were prevented by law from taking direct part in police activities such as investigations and arrests.
"It is a monumental task," said one of the officials, adding that close coordination was needed to train local emergency officials, who could in turn teach others at the local level.
"Those (cities) who have been contacted are very enthusiastic," the official said.

The programme goal this year was to complete initial assessment of emergency response capability in 27 cities by the end of September. Among cities topping the list were New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, Houston, Kansas City, San Diego, Philadelphia and Washington.

The defence officials said Congress had added legislation to the 1997 defence bill to enhance the capability of federal, state and local emergency response agencies and that the current plan was to train some 120 cities and high-population localities.
Congress was providing $42.6 million in Defence Department funds this year to begin the programme and the Clinton administration was seeking another $48.7 million in fiscal 1998.
